## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the best Fitbod alternative in 2026?

Hevy is the best all-round Fitbod alternative for most lifters: it covers logging, routines and progress charts with a generous free tier and Pro at $23.99 a year against Fitbod's $95.99. If you specifically want the workout generated for you, Boostcamp's free program library is the better swap.

### Is there a free version of Fitbod?

No. Fitbod offers three free trial workouts, or a 7-day trial through the app stores, and then requires a subscription at $15.99 a month or $95.99 a year. When the subscription lapses the app stops working, which is why FitNotes, Hevy's free tier and notes-app logging are common exits.

# 6 Best Fitbod Alternatives in 2026 (Cheaper & Ranked)

Quick answer: Hevy is the best all-round Fitbod alternative for most lifters. Boostcamp is the best free source of proven programs, FitNotes is the best truly free logger on Android, and Gym Note Plus is the fastest option if you would rather type your workouts as plain text. The right pick depends on why you are leaving. [...] Fitbod's AI is the other reason. Its generated workouts are the whole product, and lifters who follow a real program (5/3/1, GZCLP, a coach's plan) end up fighting the app to make it run someone else's plan. Reviewers make the same point: the algorithm decides, and you mostly go along with it.

Alternatives split into two camps: apps where you direct the training yourself, and apps that still hand you a plan. Know which camp you are in before you pick.

## What should you use to run your own program?

### Hevy

The best all-round replacement. Hevy does what Fitbod's logging layer does, with routines, supersets, rest timers and progress charts, and its free tier is generous enough that many lifters never pay.

results.content:
For Fitbod users specifically interested in hypertrophy rather than general fitness, Alpha Progression is more specialized: the app is built around hypertrophy programming, not general workout generation. The pricing is similar to Fitbod ($12.99/month or $79.99/year) but the science-backed plans and periodization structure feel closer to a coach-designed block than to algorithmic session generation. Apple Vision is supported.

## Dr. Muscle

### Why it's a real alternative

Dr. Muscle is the closest direct alternative to Fitbod's AI-driven workout generation. The app uses real-time AI to select exercises based on available equipment, adjust intensity based on logged performance, and adapt future sessions to your recovery and progression. The pitch is 'AI pocket personal trainer'. [...] Dr. Muscle recently introduced a free plan, with paid tiers unlocking the full feature set (real-time adjustments, nutrition guidance, full workout history charts). The premium pricing is on the higher end of the category, but for lifters who specifically valued Fitbod's algorithmic adaptation and want a more aggressive AI implementation, Dr. Muscle is the closest equivalent in the market.

## Liftosaur

### Why it's a real alternative

Liftosaur is the opposite of Fitbod's algorithm-decides-everything approach. The app is built around Liftoscript, a plain-text scripting language for defining custom workout programs with arbitrary progression rules. Pre-built programs include 5/3/1, GZCLP, and Metallicadpa PPL. [...] The core difference is the training model. Fitbod generates each session via algorithm. Boostcamp gives you a multi-week structured program (or lets you build your own, or generates one via the personalized programs feature on Pro) and tracks progress block-over-block. If you want the planning question answered by a named methodology you can name and refer back to rather than a fresh algorithm output each session, Boostcamp's model fits that better, and the free tier removes the cost question.

results.content:
### Alternatives

Fitbod is great if you need AI-generated workouts for a variety of strength training goals. However, if you’re training for a specific sport, you may find the programming somewhat problematic. Caine, an Olympian who competed at the Tokyo Games, found the programming wasn’t useful for Olympic lifting.

“The AI workouts that were generated for me seemed off,” he explained, giving the app 3 out of 5 stars for instruction. “Naturally, I chose Olympic lifting as my goal, but the weights and rep schemes seemed wildly off for a weightlifting program. I think a lot would be solved if you could put max lifts in there. Otherwise, you’re still guessing at weights and programming for yourself.” [...] Caine gave the app 5 out of 5 stars for the equipment demands, saying, “You can select the equipment you have available, ranging from access to free weights and machines to just bodyweight exercises.”

As you train, Fitbod tracks your progress and even shows a heat map of your recent training, allowing you to see which muscles have been trained.

> Using the app and logging my own workouts was easy. The questionnaire that helps program for you asks questions about your experience level, equipment available, and the type of training you are focusing on.
>
> Caine Wilkes, OLY, CNC, USAW-L1

### Alternatives [...] If you’re looking for an app that can generate endless workouts for a variety of goals tailored to your preferences and equipment, Fitbod is a great choice. It focuses on strength training workouts, allowing users to build muscle and strength or train for specific activities, such as Olympic weightlifting or powerlifting. It earns 5 out of 5 stars for workout variety, and it’s affordably priced compared to other apps.
